paras: The threatened lynching of Philander Husted took place in February 1882 at the jail where Husted, a young man of South Toledo, Ohio, was held on an accusation of raping a young girl named Long. A crowd gathered to lynch him and a rope was secured, but no attack followed, and Husted survived an attempt to take his own life. Neither report found states his race.

According to the Perrysburg journal, the girl was the 12-year-old daughter of Daniel Long, whom the paper described as 'an old and de- crepid ex-soldier.' That paper said she came to Husted's house daily for milk and that he assaulted her there on a Saturday while his family was away. A statewide news digest instead named her Nancy Long, gave her age as eleven, and said Husted went to the Long house when only she was at home.

Husted was arrested and locked up on Sunday evening. The Perrysburg journal wrote that 'the excitement had become so great that it was thought he would be taken out and lynched,' and that a rope was obtained, but 'cooler councils prevailed.' In the digest's version, people 'collected at the jail to lynch' him, and on hearing 'their clamor' he opened an artery in his arm. He had nearly bled to death before the authorities noticed, the digest said, but prompt action saved him; the local paper said only that he cut a vein and was found in time.
Husted pleaded guilty at his preliminary examination on the following Tuesday. No report of an indictment, trial or sentence, or of any action against members of the crowd, appears in the coverage.

The Perrysburg journal of Wood County ran the first report on 24 February 1882 under the heading 'Rape at South Toledo.' It treated the accusation as proven, called Husted 'a worthless wretch' and 'the worthless fiend,' and recounted the lynching plan without comment. A week later, on 2 March, the 'Ohio State News' column in the Somerset press and the Eaton Democrat opened the item with 'A HORRIBLE story comes from Maumee' and explained the crowd by saying 'so indignant were the people.' Neither version mentioned race.

The two accounts disagree on the accused man's first name (Philander or Leander), the place (South Toledo or Maumee), the girl's age (12 or eleven), whose house the assault occurred in, and whether he cut a vein or an artery. The Perrysburg journal was the earlier and more local source, while the Maumee version came from a later statewide digest.

bases: A crowd gathered at the jail to lynch a man accused of rape and a rope was secured, but no one was attacked or killed (A1, A2).
The people who 'collected at the jail to lynch' Husted acted in response to a rape accusation, but no one was killed; Husted survived both the threat and his own suicide attempt (A1, A2).

The local Perrysburg journal (A1) and the state-news digest (A2) differ in names, age and place in ways that suggest separate sourcing, and agree on the accusation, the jailing, the lynching threat and the cut arm.

accounts.label: State-news digest
accounts.gist: Husted went to the Long house when only Nancy was home; when people collected at the jail to lynch him he opened an artery on hearing their clamor and was saved by prompt action.

framing.detail: The Perrysburg journal headed the item 'Rape at South Toledo', treated the accusation as fact, called Husted 'a worthless wretch' and 'the worthless fiend', and reported the lynching plan without criticism.
The 'Ohio State News' digest called it 'A HORRIBLE story', explained the crowd as 'so indignant were the people', and treated the accusation as fact.
